input: In today's competitive manufacturing environment, maintaining high product quality is crucial, and a recent defect-reduction project on the packing line has delivered noteworthy results in this regard. Over the course of one quarter, the project successfully reduced the reject rate from 3.2% to 2.1%, representing a reduction of 1.1 percentage points that underscores the effectiveness of the improvement work undertaken. It is important to note that the reject rate serves as a key indicator of line performance, expressing the proportion of packed units that are rejected, and the figures discussed here compare the quarterly rates for the same line before and after the changes were implemented. When this reduction of 1.1 percentage points is considered against the line's annual volume of 326k units per year, it translates into approximately 3586 fewer rejected units per year, highlighting the tangible operational benefit of the improvement. This figure should be understood as an annualised estimate rather than a count of units already saved, as it applies the measured quarterly improvement to a full year at the stated volume, and it would naturally be lower in a year with reduced throughput. It is also worth noting that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown of the line, and the rates have not been adjusted for this shutdown, meaning that the shutdown period forms part of the measurement window and its influence has not been separated out. Overall, the project demonstrates a reduction of 1.1 percentage points in the reject rate, worth about 3586 avoided rejected units annually at 326k units per year, subject to the caveat regarding the unadjusted shutdown.
